bodyMarkdown:
## The idea in plain language

Six people around a circular table, and clues about who sits next to whom. The thing that makes circular arrangements different from a straight line is that there is no first or last seat — only neighbours.

So fix somebody's position arbitrarily and arrange everyone else relative to them. Rotating the whole table does not create a new arrangement.

## What is actually going on

Draw the actual shape — a circle with the right number of seats, or a row of boxes. Do not try to hold it in your head.

Fix one person to break the rotational symmetry. Then place the most rigid clue next: 'X sits immediately left of Y' is far more restrictive than 'X sits somewhere opposite Y'.

Direction matters enormously in circular puzzles. Decide once whether people face the centre or outwards, since that flips what 'left' means, and write it at the top of your diagram.

## Choosing whether to attempt a set

Before solving anything, spend 30 seconds deciding whether to attempt the set at all. Count how many questions it carries, look at whether the data is fully given or has to be deduced, and check whether the first question is answerable from a single row or needs the whole grid solved. A set that takes 12 minutes for 4 marks is worse than two sets that take 5 minutes each. Walking away from a bad set is a skill, not a failure.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Five people sit in a circle. B is immediately clockwise of A. C is directly opposite... with 5 seats, why is that impossible?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
With an odd number of seats, no seat has a true opposite — the position directly across falls between two seats.

'Directly opposite' clues only make sense when the number of seats is even.

Spotting that immediately tells you the clue must mean something else, or the set has a different seat count than assumed.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: Checking whether opposites can even exist takes two seconds and prevents a lot of wasted effort.

formulaCards.title: Fix one, arrange the rest
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: In a circle, fix one person to remove rotational duplicates. $n$ people in a circle have $(n-1)!$ distinct arrangements.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: 5 people around a table have $4! = 24$ arrangements, not 120.

formulaCards.title: Opposites need even seats
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: A seat has a directly opposite seat only when the total number of seats is even.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: In 8 seats, seat 1 faces seat 5. In 7 seats, nothing faces seat 1 exactly.

commonTraps: Forgetting to state whether people face inward or outward, which reverses left and right.
Treating rotations of the same arrangement as different answers.
Applying 'directly opposite' logic to an odd number of seats.
